'''Allison A. Campbell''' (born 1963, in [[Portland, Oregon]])<ref name=MacDermott/> is an American [[chemist]] who is known in the areas of [[biomineralization]], [[biomimetics]] and [[biomaterials]] for her innovative work on bioactive coatings for medical implants.  She is the acting associate laboratory director for the Earth and Biological Sciences Directorate<ref name=Meachem/> at the [[Pacific Northwest National Laboratory]] (PNNL) of the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]]. She previously served as director of the Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory (EMSL) at PNNL.  She was elected as the 2017 president of the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS).<ref name=Wang>{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Linda|title=Allison Campbell Wins ACS President-Elect|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=November 9, 2015|volume=93|issue=44|page=5|doi=10.1021/cen-09344-notw1 |url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/93/i44/Allison-Campbell-Wins-ACS-President.html|accessdate=20 January 2016|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=ACS2015>{{cite web|title=PNNL chemist Allison Campbell elected 2017 president of world's largest scientific society|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2015/november/pnnl-chemist-allison-campbell-elected-2017-president-of-worlds-largest-scientific-society.html|website=ACS Chemistry for Life|publisher=American Chemical Society|accessdate=20 January 2016|ref=November 5, 2015}}</ref>

==Education==
Campbell grew up in [[Portland, Oregon]], in a medical family: her father was a [[pediatric surgeon]] and her mother a medical technician.<ref name=Bisco/> Campbell received a Bachelor of Arts degree in chemistry from [[Gettysburg College]] in [[Pennsylvania]] in 1985.<ref name=Meachem>{{cite web|last1=Meachem|first1=Erin|title=Allison Campbell '85 named president of the American Chemical Society|url=http://www.gettysburg.edu/news_events/press_release_detail.dot?id=db6a6b68-3858-4a44-a1a1-09d30435b8a3|website=News @ Gettysburg|publisher=Gettysburg College.|accessdate=20 January 2016}}</ref> She then attended the [[State University of New York at Buffalo]], working with [[George Nancollas]] to study [[biomineralization]] and the interaction of [[proteins]] with [[minerals]] at the molecular level.<ref name=Bisco/> She defended her thesis in 1990 and received  her doctorate in [[physical chemistry]] from the University at Buffalo in 1991.<ref name=Bisco>{{cite web|last1=Bisco|first1=Jim|title=Chemistry star: Allison Campbell, Ph.D. '91, one of America's top chemists, revolutionizes joint implant surgery|url=http://www.buffalo.edu/ubt/UBT-archives/22_ubtw03/alumni_profiles/|website=UB Today|publisher=University of Buffalo|accessdate=20 January 2016|date=2003|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160112084251/http://www.buffalo.edu/ubt/UBT-archives/22_ubtw03/alumni_profiles/|archive-date=12 January 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==

In 1990 Campbell began a postdoctoral fellowship in the material sciences department of the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) in Richland, Washington. In 1992 she joined their staff as a research scientist.  She applied techniques for growing thin films on surfaces to the development of bioactive coatings. Campbell's bioceramics promote the growth of a [[calcium phosphate]] layer over implant surfaces for artificial hip and knee implants, dental implants, and pins supporting broken bones, to prevent wear and prolong implant usability.<ref name=Bisco/><ref name=Campbell>{{cite journal|last1=Campbell|first1=Allison A.|title=Bioceramics for implant coatings|journal=Materials Today|date=November 2003|volume=6|issue=11|pages=26–30|doi=10.1016/S1369-7021(03)01128-3|doi-access=free}}</ref>  Campbell holds several patents for this new technology.<ref name=PNNLBio>{{cite web|title=Allison A. Campbell|url=http://www.pnnl.gov/about/bio/AllisonCampbell.asp|website=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory|accessdate=21 January 2016}}</ref> The coating also kills bacteria, reducing post-surgical infections. The process was licensed to Bacterin in 2004. Campbell's work was recognized with several awards.<ref name=Showalter>{{cite news|last1=Showalter|first1=Mary Ann|title=EMSL Director Wins Prestigious R&D 100 Award|url=http://www.emsl.pnl.gov/docs/inbriefs/campbellrd20060711.pdf|accessdate=21 January 2016|work=EMSL in Brief|date=July 10, 2006}}</ref>

In 1994, she was an invited researcher at the Research Group on Mechanics of Heterogeneous Solids of the [[Max Planck Society]] at the [[Dresden University of Technology|Technische Universität Dresden]], [[Germany]].<ref name=MacDermott/>  She has taught at [[Whitman College]], [[Walla Walla, Washington]] (1999) and at the [[University of Washington]] (2000-2008).<ref name=MacDermott/>

In 2000, Campbell became associate director of the [[Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory]] (EMSL) at PNNL, followed by interim director in 2004 and director in 2005.<ref name=PNNLBio/> As a scientific user facility, EMSL's facilities are used by hundreds of scientists from around the world each year.  Under Campbell's directorship, EMSL Campbell substantially expanded EMSL's resources, adding 32 scientific instruments at a cost of $60 million, expanding computing and office space, and opening a $7 million "Quiet Wing" and a Radiochemistry Annex.<ref name=EMSLBio>{{cite web|title=Allison Campbell|url=https://www.emsl.pnl.gov/emslweb/people/allison-campbell|website=EMSL|accessdate=21 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150525022821/http://www.emsl.pnl.gov/emslweb/people/allison-campbell|archive-date=25 May 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Campbell is an associate laboratory director for the Earth and Biological Sciences Directorate<ref name=Meachem/> at the [[Pacific Northwest National Laboratory]] (PNNL) of the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]], where she leads over 500 researchers and staff. She also oversees the [[Atmospheric Radiation Measurement]] (ARM) and [[Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory]] (EMSL) facilities of the Department of Energy.<ref name=Rickey>{{cite web|last=Rickey|first=Tom|title=PNNL chemist elected president-elect of American Chemical Society Allison Campbell to lead world's largest scientific society|url=http://www.pnnl.gov/news/release.aspx?id=4231|website=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory|date=November 3, 2015|accessdate=21 January 2016}}</ref>  Their scientific work covers a broad range of initiatives in bioenergy, microbiology, biomedical science, environmental recovery, and climate science.<ref name=Key2015>{{cite web|title=2015 Key Accomplishments|url=http://www.pnnl.gov/science/pdf/FCSD_FY15_Key_Accomp_web.pdf|website=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory|accessdate=21 January 2016}}</ref>

==Advocacy==
Campbell advocates for federal support of science and chemistry research and education.<ref name=Statement/>  On September 10, 2009, she testified to the [[United States House Committee on Science, Space and Technology]]'s Subcommittee on Energy & Environment, as part of a Witness Panel discussion on ''Biological Research for Energy and Medical Applications at the Department of Energy Office of Science''.<ref name=Committee>{{cite web|title=Biological Research for Energy and Medical Applications at the Department of Energy Office of Science|url=http://archives.democrats.science.house.gov/publications/hearings_markups_details.aspx?NewsID=2587|website=Committee on Science, Space and Technology|publisher=U. S. House of Representatives|accessdate=21 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160907012542/http://archives.democrats.science.house.gov/publications/hearings_markups_details.aspx?NewsID=2587|archive-date=7 September 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>  She is a member of the Chemical Sciences Roundtable of the [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine]].<ref name=CSR>{{cite web|title=CSR Members|url=http://dels.nas.edu/global/bcst/Csr-Members.xml|website=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine|accessdate=21 January 2016}}</ref>  As the 2017 president of the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS) she has said she will work to educate both politicians and the public on the importance of the sciences as "potent forces for good in our world".<ref name=Wang/><ref name=ACS2015/><ref name=Statement/>

{{blockquote|Science has become politicized to an unprecedented degree in the U.S. ACS has a central role to play in educating policy-makers and the public on the real contributions that chemistry makes every moment of every day to our high quality of life.|Allison Campbell, 2015<ref name=Statement/>}}

==Awards and honors==
Campbell has received a number of awards and honors including the following:

* 2013, Gettysburg College Distinguished Alumni Award<ref name=Commencement>{{cite news|title=Outstanding alumni honored on Commencement and Reunion weekends|url=http://www.gettysburg.edu/news_events/press_release_detail.dot?id=119576cf-4691-4aee-b5da-35638c7e78e3|accessdate=21 January 2016|work=News@Gettysburg|agency=Gettysburg University|date=5 June 2013}}</ref>
* 2012, Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS)<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Allison Campbell '85 named American Association for the Advancement of Science Fellow|url=http://www.gettysburg.edu/alumni2/explore/press-release-detail.dot?id=343250d2-29fd-4b54-a399-1caca709b48f|website=Gettysburg College|date=17 January 2013|accessdate=20 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160113220035/http://www.gettysburg.edu/alumni2/explore/press-release-detail.dot?id=343250d2-29fd-4b54-a399-1caca709b48f|archive-date=13 January 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2011, Pioneer of Science Award (with George Nancollas), from [[Hauptman-Woodward Medical Research Institute]] in Buffalo, New York<ref name=Pioneer>{{cite web|last1=Beckman|first1=Mary|title=PNNL's Allison Campbell honored for work in tooth formation, artificial bone EMSL Director presented Pioneer of Science Award for scientific, mentoring contributions|url=http://www.pnnl.gov/news/release.aspx?id=895|website=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory|publisher=October 26, 2011|accessdate=21 January 2016}}</ref> 
* 2006, R&D 100 Award from ''R&D Magazine''<ref name=Showalter/>
* 2006, Federal Laboratory Consortium Award for Technology Transfer<ref name=Showalter/>
* 2003, George W. Thorn Award from the [[State University of New York at Buffalo]] Alumni Association<ref name=Bisco/>
* 2002,  12 Women at the Forefront of Chemistry, in celebration of the 75th anniversary of the ACS Women Chemist Committee<ref name=Bisco/> (profiled in ''[[Chemical & Engineering News]]'')<ref name=MacDermott>{{cite journal|last1=MacDermott|first1=Kevin|title=Women in Chemistry: Leading by Example|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=February 25, 2002|volume=80|issue=8|page=31|doi=10.1021/cen-v080n008.p031}}</ref>
* 1984,  Member of the [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name=Statement>{{cite journal|title=For President-Elect 2016 Allison A. Campbell, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, WA|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=November 9, 2015|volume=93|issue=36|page=46|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/93/i36/President-Elect-AllisonCampbell.html|accessdate=20 January 2016}}</ref>

==Other interests ==
Campbell represented the U.S. as an [[Equestrianism|equestrienne]] in the Junior World Championships in 1987. She was also a contender for the U.S. Olympic equestrian team in 1988.<ref name=MacDermott/><ref name=Bisco/> Campbell has also advocated for greater [[LGBTQIA+]] inclusion and support within STEM.

==Personal life==
Campbell lives in Washington state with her wife, Julie.<ref name=C&EN>{{cite web|last=Campbell|first=Allison|title=Pedaling the power of chemistry|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i1/Pedaling-power-chemistry.html|date=January 2, 2017|accessdate=January 8, 2021}}</ref> She is an avid cyclist and fly-fishing enthusiast.<ref name=C&EN/>
